title: AI-Powered Automated Underwater Marine Debris and Anomaly Detection System using Side-Scan Sonar Imagery
description:
• Background The accumulation of anthropogenic (man-made) debris in marine ecosystems poses a critical threat to global biodiversity. Among the most destructive types of pollution are ‘ghost nets’-abandoned, lost, or discarded fishing gear. These nets continuously trap and kill marine life,destroy coral reefs, and damage commercial vessel propellers.
Because the ocean is vast and dark, marine conservationists and underwater technologists rely on Side Scan Sonar (SSS) instruments. These sensors are towed behind ships or mounted on Autonomous Underwater Vehicles (AUVs) to create detailed acoustic maps of the seafloor.However, manual inspection of thousands of kilometers of sonar logs is incredibly slow, tedious, and prone to human error. Debris can easily blend into natural geological features like rock formations, sand ripples, and marine ridges. Automating this process via computer vision is essential for efficient ocean cleanup operations.
• Description Participants must develop an end-to-end automated computer vision pipeline capable of ingesting side-scan sonar imagery, identifying man-made debris against a complex natural background, and generating actionable localized data.The software system must be robust enough to handle the core challenges inherent to acoustic imagery: high speckle noise, varying pixel resolutions, acoustic shadows, and data dropouts caused by underwater vehicle motion (heave, pitch, and roll). The primary objective is to build an algorithm that reliably separates natural seafloor topology from artificial anomalies. The final solution should be optimized to run efficiently, potentially allowing deployment on edge devices or onboard a marine drone without requiring heavy cloud computing dependencies.
• Expected Solution Teams are expected to deliver a functional, modular software prototype containing the following core components:
• Object Detection / Semantic Segmentation Model: An AI/ML architecture (such as YOLO,Faster R-CNN, or U-Net) trained to detect and draw bounding boxes or pixel-level masks around man-made objects (including shipwrecks, pipes, cylinders, and entangled debris nets).
• Confidence Scoring & Noise Filtering Module: An algorithmic pipeline or pre-processing filter that minimizes false positives caused by natural acoustic shadows or rock clusters,outputting a clear confidence score (0% to 100%) for every detected anomaly.
• Anomalous Reporting & Geotagging Engine: A data-parsing script or lightweight dashboard interface that reads sonar metadata (such as coordinate files or ping headers) to output a structured report (JSON or CSV format). This report must detail the exact location (latitude/longitude), bounding dimensions, and classification of each detected hazard.
• User Interface (UI) Dashboard: A visual interface where a user can upload a raw sonar image log, view the AI models' detections overlaid on the map in real-time, and download the generated anomaly reports.
summary: Innovation (5/5): draws on ai, ml, computer vision applied to a renewable / sustainable energy problem, placing it in the breakthrough band. Feasibility (3/5): as a software build with moderate integration complexity, a full build is tight for 36 hours and will need scope-cutting. Impact (2/5): addresses a more targeted user group within Renewable / Sustainable Energy. Tech Depth (5/5): centers on model, real-time, algorithm. Sustainability (3/5): will need a maintenance/upkeep plan post-hackathon. Scalability (4/5): built to extend across states/users with modest rework. Total 22/30 -> Green verdict.

detail.title: AI-Powered Automated Underwater Marine Debris and Anomaly Detection using Side-Scan Sonar

overview.in_plain_terms: Build a computer vision system that scans sonar images of the seafloor and automatically spots man-made debris, especially abandoned fishing nets, that are currently found by slowly, manually reviewing thousands of kilometers of sonar logs.
overview.why_it_matters: Ghost nets keep killing marine life and destroying reefs long after they're lost. Automating detection means cleanup efforts can actually find and target debris at the scale the ocean demands.
pain_points: Manual inspection of sonar logs across thousands of kilometers is slow, tedious, and error-prone.
Debris can visually blend into natural seafloor features (rocks, sand ripples, ridges).
No automated computer vision pipeline currently handles this specific acoustic imagery challenge.
overview.background: Ghost nets and other marine debris cause severe ecological damage, and while side-scan sonar generates the data needed to find them, manual review of the resulting acoustic imagery doesn't scale to the volume needed for effective ocean cleanup.
overview.whats_being_asked: An end-to-end computer vision pipeline ingesting side-scan sonar imagery, distinguishing man-made debris from complex natural seafloor backgrounds, and generating actionable localized detection data.
expected_solution: Automated ingestion and processing of side-scan sonar imagery.
Debris detection robust to acoustic imagery challenges (noise, shadow, resolution variability).
Discrimination between debris and natural geological features.
Actionable, localized output data for cleanup operations.

analysis.innovation_scope_note: Breakthrough. Computer vision on acoustic (not optical) imagery for this specific debris-vs-natural-feature discrimination task is a genuinely specialized, non-trivial application, sonar imagery has fundamentally different characteristics than camera imagery.
analysis.invention_effort_note: High. Requires understanding sonar imagery's unique noise/shadow characteristics plus building a genuinely discriminating classifier, more specialized than standard object detection.

competitive_landscape.note: Sonar/acoustic imagery computer vision is a specialized niche, most CV teams default to optical imagery experience, real differentiation for teams willing to engage with sonar-specific challenges.

innovation.note: Applying CV specifically to acoustic sonar imagery's unique characteristics (rather than treating it like a standard photo) is genuinely differentiating.

invention.note: Requires domain understanding of sonar imagery formation plus a real discriminating classification pipeline.

technical_feasibility.note: Some public side-scan sonar imagery datasets exist for research purposes, providing real test data without requiring actual field deployment.

impact_and_benefits.note: Genuine ecological value for ocean cleanup efforts, though a narrower, more specialized audience than broadly public-facing PS.

architecture.note: An imagery-processing and classification pipeline, well-understood pattern applied to a specialized data type.

overall_verdict.reasoning: Strong pick for a team with computer vision experience willing to genuinely engage with sonar imagery's unique characteristics rather than treating it like a standard photo classification problem. Real test data exists, making this genuinely demonstrable.

evaluator_lens.biggest_strength: Some public side-scan sonar datasets exist for research, giving real test data access without needing actual field deployment, a genuine advantage over many PS in this batch.
evaluator_lens.biggest_risk: Treating sonar imagery like a standard optical photo (ignoring its specific noise, shadow, and resolution characteristics) would produce a weak classifier that misses the actual technical challenge the PS is testing for.
evaluator_lens.validate_before_commit: Research sonar imagery's specific characteristics (acoustic shadow, speckle noise, resolution variation with range) before building your classifier, this domain understanding is what separates a genuinely good submission from a generic image classifier applied blindly.

idea_0_4: Research side-scan sonar imagery fundamentals: how acoustic shadows form, typical noise characteristics, resolution variation with distance from the sensor.
Source a public side-scan sonar dataset with debris/anomaly examples if available, or construct realistic synthetic examples grounded in real sonar imagery characteristics.
Split: one person on sonar-specific preprocessing, one on the classification/detection model.
prototype_4_22: Build sonar-specific preprocessing (noise reduction, shadow-aware feature extraction) rather than treating the imagery like a standard photo.
Build your debris detection/classification model on your sourced or constructed dataset.
Test specifically against natural-feature examples (rocks, sand ripples) that could be visually confused with debris, this discrimination is the actual hard part.
integration_22_30: Connect the full pipeline: raw sonar imagery -> preprocessing -> detection -> localized output data.
Test against your hardest confusion cases (natural features resembling debris) to measure real discriminating performance.
Build the localized output format, actionable data (coordinates, confidence) usable for actual cleanup targeting.
polish_30_36: Polish the output visualization, overlaying detected debris locations on the original sonar imagery.
Rehearse walking through a genuinely difficult case, a natural feature that could be confused with debris, and how your system correctly discriminates it.
Prepare to discuss sonar imagery's unique challenges and how your approach specifically addresses them, not generic CV.
build_plan.how_to_stand_out: Show your system correctly discriminating a genuinely tricky natural-feature-versus-debris case live, that discrimination, not just general detection, is the actual hard, differentiating problem this PS is testing for.

strengths: Real public sonar datasets exist, providing genuine test data access.
Specialized domain (acoustic imagery) offers real differentiation for teams willing to engage with its unique characteristics.
weaknesses: Requires genuine sonar-imagery domain understanding, not just standard computer vision experience, easy to underinvest in this.
Debris-versus-natural-feature discrimination in cluttered seafloor scenes is a genuinely hard classification problem.

roles_needed: Computer vision person (core, ideally with signal/acoustic imagery interest)
team_fit.ideal_ratio: CV-heavy, with real investment in understanding sonar imagery's specific characteristics rather than defaulting to standard photo-classification approaches.
team_fit.approach: Research sonar imagery fundamentals before building, this domain understanding directly improves classifier design and is what a marine-science-literate judge will probe.

ai_buildability_split.ai_can_build_fast: Standard CV model architectures adapted for the sonar imagery format.
ai_buildability_split.needs_human_judgment: Understanding sonar-specific imaging artifacts (acoustic shadow, speckle noise) well enough to design preprocessing and features that actually help discrimination, that's domain expertise, not a default CV pipeline.
ai_buildability_split.risk_of_leaning_on_ai_only: A generic image classifier applied to sonar data without understanding its unique formation characteristics would likely struggle specifically on the natural-feature-versus-debris discrimination that's the actual hard part of this problem.

data_resource_availability.status: Some public side-scan sonar research datasets exist and are usable for a credible demo, a genuine data advantage relative to many PS in this batch.
data_resource_availability.backup_plan: If specific debris-labeled sonar data isn't available, construct realistic synthetic examples grounded in real sonar imagery characteristics (acoustic shadow patterns, speckle noise) rather than generic image data.

judge_qna.question: How does your system distinguish debris from natural features that look visually similar in sonar imagery?
judge_qna.strong_answer: Walk through your specific discrimination approach, whether it's shadow-shape analysis, texture features specific to man-made materials, or a learned classifier trained on confusable examples, and show a real example of correct discrimination.
judge_qna.follow_up: What's your false-positive rate on natural features that could be mistaken for debris?

judge_qna.question: How does your model's performance change with imagery resolution, which varies with distance from the sonar sensor?
judge_qna.strong_answer: Address this directly, sonar resolution genuinely degrades with range, describe how your model handles or accounts for this variation rather than assuming uniform image quality.
judge_qna.follow_up: At what range does your model's reliability start to degrade significantly?
